entry:
French military commander and statesman, Emperor of the French (r. 1804–14, 1815). Born Napoleone di Buonaparte on the island of [[Corsica]] to a family of Italian origin, he moved to mainland France in 1779 and was commissioned in the French Royal Army in 1785. He supported the [[French Revolution|Revolution]] and rose rapidly after the siege of Toulon in 1793, then won decisive victories against the Austrians and their Italian allies in 1796. After an invasion of Egypt and Syria in 1798, he engineered the Coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799 and became First Consul. He sold Louisiana to the United States in 1803 and crowned himself emperor in December 1804.

His victory at the [[Battle of Austerlitz]] in 1805 led to the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire. He defeated Prussia at Jena–Auerstedt in 1806 and the Russians at Friedland in 1807. His invasion of the Iberian Peninsula in 1808, which installed his brother Joseph as King of Spain, provoked the [[Peninsular War]]. After the invasion of Russia in 1812 and a catastrophic winter retreat, he was decisively defeated at the [[Battle of Leipzig]] in 1813 and abdicated in April 1814, going into exile on Elba. About ten months later he escaped with around a thousand men and reclaimed France in the [[Hundred Days]], but the Seventh Coalition defeated him at the [[Battle of Waterloo]] in June 1815. He was exiled to Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, where he died.

His reforms include the [[Napoleonic Code]], a system of public education, the abolition of the vestiges of feudalism, and the emancipation of Jews and other religious minorities. Critics point to his abolition of the free press, the end of directly elected representative government, the reinstatement of slavery in French colonies, reduced civil rights for women and children, and the return of a hereditary monarchy and nobility. One estimate puts deaths from the Napoleonic Wars at 3 to 6 million. His tactics are still studied at military schools.

Account of a series of related events or experiences, real or imagined, presented through words, images, or a combination of both. Also called a story or tale. A narrative may be nonfictional, as in memoir, [[Biography|biography]], news report, or documentary, or fictional, as in the fairy tale, fable, [[Legend|legend]], thriller, or novel. It is distinguished from a simple description of qualities, states, or situations in which no particular individuals are involved.

Narrative appears in speech, [[Literature|literature]], theatre, dance, music and song, comics, [[Journalism|journalism]], animation, film, television, video games, and radio, and potentially even in static visual art such as painting and sculpture, provided a sequence of events is presented. Narratives range from a single sentence, such as "the cat sat on the mat," to long series spanning multiple books, films, or television episodes. A personal narrative is a prose account in which a speaker or writer relates their own experiences, often informally.

The social activity of sharing narratives is called storytelling, most of which has historically been oral. With the rise of literate societies, many narratives were also recorded in writing. Narration, the formal process of constructing a narrative, is one of the four traditional rhetorical modes of discourse, along with argumentation, description, and exposition.

Scholars identify basic elements of narrative, including character and conflict. Characters, who may be imaginary or based on real people, drive the plot. The protagonist is the main character, often opposed by an antagonist. In many traditional narratives the protagonist is a [[Hero|hero]] who fights for morally good causes. Conflict is the tension that drives characters' thoughts and actions, and in the narrow sense the major problem the protagonist faces. The words narration and narrative entered English from French in the 15th century and derive from the Latin *narrare* ("to tell").

Large community whose members share a collective identity based on features such as language, history, ethnicity, culture, territory, and society. Some nations are constructed around ethnicity (ethnic nationalism), while others are bound by political constitutions (civic nationalism). A nation is generally more overtly political than an [[Ethnicity|ethnic group]], and what distinguishes it from other forms of collective identity, according to Thomas Hylland Eriksen, is its relationship with the state.

Benedict Anderson defined a nation as "an imagined political community," imagined because even members of the smallest nation will never know most of their fellow members. Anthony D. Smith defined nations as cultural-political communities that have become conscious of their autonomy, unity, and particular interests. Black's Law Dictionary describes a community of people inhabiting a defined territory and organized under an independent government, so that nation can be synonymous with [[State (polity)|state]] or country. A nation differs from a state in that it emphasizes sociocultural cohesion, which may not align with political boundaries, producing multinational states and stateless nations.

The consensus among scholars is that nations are socially constructed, historically contingent, and a distinctly modern phenomenon. [[Nationalism]], the belief that state and nation should align, did not become a prominent ideology until the end of the 18th century. Some historians nonetheless trace nations to the medieval period or antiquity. Smith argued that only Egypt and Judah, at certain periods, approximated true nations in the ancient world. Adrian Hastings argued that English nationhood goes back to [[Alfred the Great]]'s struggle against Norse invaders, a view John Breuilly criticized for assuming that continued use of a term means continuity of meaning.

The English word comes from Middle English *nacioun*, from Old French and from Latin *natio*, from *nasci* ("to be born"). [[Cicero]] used *natio* for "people."

Ideology or movement holding that the [[Nation|nation]] should be congruent with the state. As a movement, it tends to promote the interests of a particular nation, especially to gain and maintain its [[Sovereignty|sovereignty]] over a perceived homeland and create a nation-state. It holds that the nation should govern itself free from outside interference, that it is a natural and ideal basis for a polity, and that it is the only rightful source of political power. It also seeks a single national identity built on shared culture, ethnicity, homeland, language, religion, traditions, or belief in a shared history, and promotes national unity.

Definitions of "nation" differ, producing different types of nationalism. The two main forms are ethnic nationalism and civic nationalism, though this dichotomy has been criticized as an oversimplification. Nationalism can combine with diverse ideologies, such as [[Conservatism|conservatism]] (national conservatism and right-wing populism) or socialism (left-wing nationalism). The moral value of nationalism, its relation to patriotism, and its compatibility with cosmopolitanism are subjects of philosophical debate.

The word nation was applied before 1800 in Europe to the inhabitants of a country and to collective identities that could include shared history, law, language, and religion. In the early 17th century [[Hugo Grotius]] refined the terminology of nations and sovereignty. The term nationalism dates to around 1798 and became more negative in its connotations after 1914. Benedict Anderson linked its rise to print capitalism and printed media in vernacular languages. From the late 18th century, particularly with the [[French Revolution]], the principle of popular sovereignty spread. Modernization theory, currently the most commonly accepted explanation, holds that industrialization, urbanization, and mass education made national consciousness possible. Primordialism, which held that nations have always existed, has been rejected by most scholars.

Nationalism is judged positive or negative depending on its ideology and outcomes. Supporters point to its role in movements for freedom and justice, in cultural revivals, and in national unification. Critics note that it has been used to legitimize racial, ethnic, and religious divisions, suppress minorities, and start wars, and it is frequently cited as a cause of both world wars.

Severely harmful impact on a society or community caused by a natural phenomenon or hazard. Examples of natural hazards include avalanches, droughts, earthquakes, floods, heat waves, landslides, tropical cyclones, volcanic activity, and wildfires, as well as blizzards, dust storms, hail, ice storms, sinkholes, thunderstorms, tornadoes, and tsunamis. Disasters can cause loss of life, property damage, and economic damage. The extent depends on how well people are prepared and how strong buildings, roads, and other structures are.

A hazard is the threat of an event likely to have a negative impact; a disaster is the harm that follows when a hazard significantly affects a community. The U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency illustrates the distinction with the 1906 San Francisco earthquake: the earthquake was the hazard, and the resulting damage the disaster. Hazards are commonly grouped as geophysical, meteorological, hydrological, climatological, and, in some classifications, biological. FEMA's National Risk Index includes 18 natural hazards.

Many scholars argue that the term "natural disaster" is a misnomer, a criticism made as early as 1976, and should be replaced by "disaster" with the type of hazard specified. In this view a disaster arises when a hazard meets a vulnerable community, and human choices shape the outcome. Inadequate building norms, marginalization of people, poor land-use planning, overexploitation of resources, and extreme urban sprawl can cause or worsen disasters. Critics of the term say that calling disasters natural suggests the results are inevitable and obscures political and financial responsibility for risk reduction, compensation, and insurance. Climate change also affects how often extreme-weather hazards occur.

Many developing countries lack proper disaster risk reduction systems and are more vulnerable than high-income countries. As of 2019, the countries with the highest share of disability-adjusted life years lost to natural disasters were the Bahamas, Haiti, Zimbabwe, and Armenia. The Asia-Pacific region is the most disaster-prone in the world. In 2012 there were 905 natural disasters worldwide, 93% of them weather-related, with overall costs of US$170 billion.

Gaseous fossil fuel occurring naturally in geological formations, also called gas, methane gas, or fossil gas. It is a mixture of hydrocarbons, primarily methane, with small amounts of higher alkanes and traces of carbon dioxide, nitrogen, hydrogen sulfide, and helium. Methane is colorless and odorless, so a commercial odorizer such as methanethiol, which smells of rotten eggs, is added to make leaks detectable.

Natural gas forms when layers of organic matter, primarily marine microorganisms, are thermally decomposed without oxygen under intense heat and pressure over millions of years. It is often found alongside coal and petroleum and is frequently a byproduct of oil production, where it may be vented, flared, or collected. Before use it must be processed to remove impurities such as water, hydrogen sulfide, carbon dioxide, and sometimes helium and nitrogen; the processing yields ethane, propane, butanes, and pentanes. It travels by pipeline, and inter-country transport and long-term storage became widely available only with liquefied natural gas.

The gas was called "natural" in the early 1800s to distinguish it from manufactured coal gas. Chinese drillers were using gas from brine wells by about 400 BC, carrying it through bamboo pipes to boil salt water in Sichuan. In the United States, William Hart dug the first commercial well in 1821 at Fredonia, New York, leading in 1858 to the Fredonia Gas Light Company. Long-distance pipelines grew from the 1920s onward.

Burning natural gas emits fewer toxic air pollutants, less carbon dioxide, and almost no particulate matter than other fossil fuels. Critics note that venting and fugitive methane emissions can give it a similar or greater carbon footprint overall, since methane is the second-greatest greenhouse gas after carbon dioxide. Some organizations therefore prefer the terms "fossil gas" or "methane gas." Supporters stress its role in displacing coal and oil and in supplying dispatchable energy; leading producers include the United States, Russia, and Qatar.

Number used for counting, for indexing positions in a sequence, and for labeling. The natural numbers are 1, 2, 3, and so on, or, depending on convention, begin with 0. Other terms include positive integers, non-negative integers, whole numbers, and counting numbers. Whether to include 0 has no universal agreement, with set theory often including it and elementary arithmetic often excluding it. The set is commonly denoted by a bold N or a blackboard bold ℕ.

Natural numbers express two related ideas. As cardinal numbers they give the size of a collection, as in "there are seven days in a week." Two finite collections have the same cardinality if their objects can be put in one-to-one correspondence. As ordinal numbers they give position in a sequence, as in "the third day of the month." Natural numbers are the most common labels for infinite sequences because they form the simplest infinite well-ordered set. They are written with ten digits (0 to 9), and numerals can also serve as nominal numbers, identifiers with no mathematical properties, such as jersey numbers.

Natural numbers can be compared by size and arranged in a total order. Two basic operations, addition and multiplication, are defined on them and are closed, commutative, and associative, with multiplication distributing over addition. The inverse operations, subtraction and division, only sometimes give natural-number results: subtracting a larger number from a smaller one yields a negative number, and division commonly leaves a remainder. The fundamental theorem of arithmetic states that every natural number greater than 1 factors uniquely into primes.

The natural numbers can be formalized with the Peano axioms, in which an initial element and a successor function generate each subsequent number, together with the principle of mathematical induction. Giuseppe Peano axiomatized them in 1889. The integers, rational numbers, real numbers, and complex numbers are defined successively from them. Arithmetic, number theory, and combinatorics build on the natural numbers.

Material drawn from nature and used with few modifications, valued for commercial, industrial, aesthetic, scientific, or cultural purposes. On Earth, natural resources include sunlight, atmosphere, water, land, all minerals, and all vegetation and wildlife. Every man-made product is composed of natural resources at its fundamental level. A resource may exist as a separate entity, such as freshwater or a fish, or be transformed by extractive industries into a useful form, as with metal ores, rare-earth elements, petroleum, and timber.

Resources are classified by several criteria. By origin, biotic resources come from the biosphere and have life, such as flora, fauna, and fisheries; fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum are included because they form from decayed organic matter. Abiotic resources come from non-living material, including land, water, air, and ores of metals such as gold, iron, copper, and silver. By stage of development, they are potential, actual, reserves, or stocks. By renewability, renewable resources such as solar energy, air, and water can be replenished naturally, though many can be depleted by overuse; they count as renewable while replenishment exceeds consumption. Non-renewable resources, notably minerals and fossil fuels, form over long geological periods. Metals can be recycled, but coal and petroleum cannot. By ownership, resources are individual, community, national, or international.

Extraction withdraws resources from nature, from traditional preindustrial use to global industry. Extractive industries, such as hunting, trapping, mining, oil and gas drilling, and forestry, along with agriculture, form the basis of the primary sector of the economy. Resources can be a substantial part of a country's wealth.

Allocation of resources can be at the center of economic and political confrontations within and between countries, particularly during scarcity. Extraction is also a major source of human rights violations and environmental damage. International agendas, including the Sustainable Development Goals, focus on more sustainable extraction, and some scholars promote circular economy models built on reuse and recycling. Others argue that predictions of long-term depletion have often proven overstated because of substitution and efficiency gains.

Elastic polymer of isoprene harvested as latex from certain plants, chiefly the Pará rubber tree. Also called India rubber, caoutchouc, or Amazonian rubber. It consists of [[Polymer|polymers]] of isoprene with minor impurities and is classed as an elastomer. Latex, a sticky, milky colloid, is drawn off by cutting the bark in a process called tapping and refined for commercial processing. In most useful forms it has a large stretch ratio and high resilience, and it is buoyant and waterproof. Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Cambodia are leading producers.

The main commercial source is *Hevea brasiliensis*, a member of the spurge family ([[Euphorbiaceae]]), native to Brazil and now pan-tropical. Congo rubber came from *Landolphia* vines. Other sources include the rubber fig, guayule, which is prized for its hypoallergenic properties, and the Kazakh dandelion (*Taraxacum kok-saghyz*). Research in [[Nazi Germany]] on dandelion rubber failed, but in 2013 German scientists developed a cultivar that seems suitable for commercial production.

The first users were the indigenous cultures of [[Mesoamerica]]: the Olmec made rubber balls for the ballgame, and the Aztecs made containers and waterproofed textiles. Charles Marie de La Condamine brought samples to the Académie Royale des Sciences in 1736. In 1770 [[Joseph Priestley]] observed that rubber removed pencil marks, hence the name. Charles Goodyear redeveloped vulcanization in 1839, though Mesoamericans had used stabilized rubber as early as 1600 BC.

South America supplied most rubber for much of the 19th century. In 1876 Henry Wickham smuggled 70,000 seeds of the Amazonian rubber tree from Brazil to Kew Gardens, England; only 2,400 germinated. Seedlings went to India, Ceylon, the [[Dutch East Indies]], Singapore, and British Malaya, which became the biggest producer. In the early 1900s the [[Congo Free State]] was also a significant source, with latex mostly gathered by forced labor under King Leopold II. Demand outstripped natural supply by the end of the 19th century, leading to the chemical synthesis of synthetic rubber in 1909.

Astronomical body that orbits a [[Planet|planet]], [[Dwarf planet|dwarf planet]], or small Solar System body, or sometimes another natural satellite. Natural satellites are colloquially called moons, after the [[Moon]], Earth's natural satellite. In English, "Moon" capitalized denotes Earth's satellite, while lowercase "moon" is used generically.

In the Solar System there are six planetary satellite systems, comprising 456 natural satellites with confirmed orbits. Seven objects commonly considered dwarf planets also have satellites: Orcus, Pluto, Haumea, Quaoar, Makemake, Gonggong, and Eris. In all, 656 minor planets are known or suspected to have natural satellites.

The Moon was considered a planet until Copernicus published *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium* in 1543. Galileo called the moons he discovered in 1610 *Planetæ* ("planets"). The German astronomer [[Johannes Kepler]] was the first to use the term satellite for orbiting bodies, in 1610, deriving it from the [[Latin]] *satelles*, meaning "guard," "attendant," or "companion." After the launch of Sputnik in 1957, "satellite" became linked with artificial objects, and "moon" regained respectability as a term interchangeable with natural satellite.

No lower size limit for a moon is established. Objects as small as a kilometer across have been considered moons, and smaller bodies within Saturn's rings have been called moonlets. The upper limit is vague: the Earth–Moon system is sometimes described as a double planet, and some authors regard the Pluto–Charon system as a double dwarf planet because its barycenter lies above the surface of the larger body. The barycenter of every planetary moon system lies within the host planet's radius.

Regular satellites, which orbit close to the planet on prograde, uninclined circular orbits, are generally thought to have formed from the same collapsing region of the protoplanetary disk as their primary. Irregular satellites, on distant, inclined, eccentric, or retrograde orbits, are thought to be captured asteroids. The Moon and the moons of Pluto are thought to have originated from collisions of two large protoplanetary objects. [[Triton (moon)|Triton]] is large and in a close, circular orbit, but its motion is retrograde and it is thought to be a captured dwarf planet.
